item.title: As Millions of Birds Migrate, Residents Are Asked to Turn Off the Lights
item.description:
By Ishani Desai

More than 300 million birds are expected to soar across the United States on Saturday during their annual fall migration, prompting requests for residents to turn off or dim lights to help ensure their safe flight.

Hundreds of species of birds, such as blackpoll warblers, chimney swifts and scissor-tailed flycatchers, will fly from the Northern Hemisphere to South America for a warmer climate filled with more food, said Dylan Osterhaus, a postdoctoral research assistant at Purdue University who studies migratory birds.

“It’s always like Christmas morning, going out each morning and seeing what new presents arrived from the north,” he said.

But the trek can be dangerous.

At least one billion birds die each year after crashing into skyscrapers and other lighted buildings, said Adriaan Dokter, a research associate who leads Cornell University’s BirdCast, an online resource that tracks the birds in real time.

The birds, which typically travel after darkness falls, will be most heavily concentrated in eastern Minnesota and Michigan on Saturday.

The birds could fly through Illinois and Indiana and then cluster in the Southern states before soaring out of the country, according to projections from the Aeroecology Lab at Purdue University.

Some cities, such as Minneapolis and Chicago, ask residents to turn off or dim lights so the birds do not mistakenly fly toward lit structures.

Building owners or managers could switch off exterior decorative lighting and floodlights and install automatic motion sensors, the Audubon Society said. The lighting should be turned off or reduced from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The leading cause of death for wild birds is crashing into buildings, said Jessica Wilson, the executive director of the NYC Bird Alliance.

Some birds become disoriented during bad weather and can fly into tall buildings. Some migrators also are drawn into well-lit areas and cannot see glass, Dr. Dokter said.

The fall migration, which began in mid-August, could peak over next two weeks, with more than 500 million birds dotting the Northern Hemisphere, Dr. Osterhaus said. The migration period typically ends in mid-November.

The birds rely on weather patterns to determine when to fly, Dr. Dokter said. They can halt their migration if storms settle over a region.

The bird projections studied by researchers at Purdue and Cornell rely on weather radar data, Dr. Osterhaus said.

Certain weather conditions, such as favorable wind shifts, have correlated to instances in which large flocks of birds take off, he said.

Scientists have combined decades of this weather data and built a predictive model to project how many birds will be flying based on how the weather shifts, he said.

Each species has its own migration pattern.

Some species, such as the dark-eyed junco, nest in Canada and then fly in the winter to the United States, Dr. Osterhaus said.

“These birds are really trying to maximize their survival and fitness,” he said.

Generally, the fall migration contains more birds because the summer’s breeding season has concluded, said Catherine Quayle, the communications director for the Wild Bird Fund, a nonprofit that rehabilitates injured or sickened birds and other animals.

From Sept. 5 until Friday, the Wild Bird Fund admitted 453 birds, of which 124 had crashed into windows, she said. The birds cannot tell the difference between a real tree and the reflection of a tree.

In New York City, more than 250,000 birds die each year after crashing into buildings, Ms. Wilson said.

Residents can help by sticking films with patterns on windows to make the glass less clear, Dr. Dokter said.

Alexandra E. Petri contributed reporting.

item.title: Obama Urges Democrats to Move A.I. Oversight to the Center of Their Agenda
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama warned during a recent private fund-raising event that artificial intelligence technology could be “dangerous” if not properly managed, as he implored Democrats to aggressively develop political and governing agendas to prioritize the issue in the coming years.

In his remarks on Thursday, which have not been previously reported, Mr. Obama urged House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, to assemble a clear framework for a public conversation about A.I. policy, should Democrats win back the House in the midterm elections, according to a partial transcript provided by Mr. Obama’s office.

He also suggested that candidates running for president in 2028 ought to make A.I. one of their “central agendas” and “have a very clear plan” for responding to safety and economic concerns around the technology.

The recommendations from the former president amount to some of his most detailed comments yet about A.I. as a political issue for his party. At a moment when President Trump continues to downplay concerns about the technology, some Democrats see an opportunity for the party to draw a clear contrast in the midterms and beyond on an issue of growing significance. In a Democratic Party with no clear leader, many look to Mr. Obama for guidance, and his comments carry considerable weight.

The remarks come amid escalating worries about the risks associated with A.I. development, as well as growing calls for lawmakers and politicians to do more to tackle the topic. Some A.I. industry leaders are now calling for a slowdown after a summer in which swarms of misaligned A.I. agents broke free from their containers and proceeded to scheme against their owners, cheat on tests and hack outside companies.

At the fund-raiser on Thursday, a closed-door event in Manhattan organized by the campaign arm of House Democrats, Mr. Obama and Mr. Jeffries spoke for nearly an hour in front of party donors and lawmakers, according to four people familiar with the event, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private gathering.

“Once you are speaker, I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” Mr. Obama told Mr. Jeffries, according to the transcript. Mr. Jeffries had asked him a question about how Democrats should address A.I. in a Congress that has taken little action on the issue, according to two of the people.

“This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Mr. Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.”

The former president often spoke in general terms on Thursday, rather than drilling down on specific policies, according to the transcript. And he planted himself firmly in a middle ground in the heated debate over A.I., saying he considered himself neither an “accelerationist” nor a “doomer.”

One challenge facing Democrats as they chart a path forward on A.I. is speaking in one voice on the issue. The tug of war over how to regulate A.I. has been more divisive among Democrats than Republicans, who are generally more in alignment. Some Democratic politicians have called for more A.I. regulation, while others have received millions of dollars in support from groups tied to the industry’s biggest players.

A.I. is becoming a larger part of the country’s political calculus heading into the midterms. This year’s elections have been flooded with money from A.I. companies and allied groups. And anxiety about the technology, a rare issue that many Republican and Democratic voters can agree on, has peaked in recent days after a researcher at the A.I. company Anthropic loudly and publicly resigned, writing in a viral social media post that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Mr. Jeffries explicitly mentioned the resignation in his question to Mr. Obama, according to one of the people familiar with the event.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of the A.I. company Anthropic, called for a global slowdown of A.I. development in a 3,800-word essay published on Saturday. Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, and Elon Musk, whose SpaceX rocket company has been ramping up spending on A.I., quickly wrote in social media posts that they agreed with him.

The White House has long maintained an unabashedly accelerationist stance. Mr. Trump recently told reporters he didn’t have “any” concerns about A.I.’s risks — just about falling behind to competitors like China. He has said that those who oppose A.I. data centers must prefer to be “backwards and poor.”

“President Obama is correct that decisive action must be taken on artificial intelligence,” Mr. Jeffries said in a statement, adding that “Republicans have abdicated their responsibility to govern on behalf of the American people. We will not repeat their error.”

On Capitol Hill, where little has been done to regulate A.I., some Democrats have been circulating a letter urging Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, to stop members from going home on recess until they pass A.I. safeguards.

Many Republicans want action, too. Several have introduced bipartisan A.I. legislation, and Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida has called for a special session on the topic. A growing number of Republicans are campaigning against data centers, in addition to many Democrats.

After Mr. Johnson became speaker in 2023, Republican leadership declined to renew a bipartisan task force on A.I. In response, Democrats formed their own A.I. commission, which is now putting the finishing touches on a policy framework. That framework is expected to be released this fall after some final checks by Mr. Jeffries, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Mr. Obama has taken a special interest in A.I. in recent years, and he has offered himself as a sounding board to industry leaders, according to two people familiar with his conversations. Those leaders include Mr. Altman and Mr. Amodei, according to one of the people. Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.

Now, Mr. Obama wants to help guide the Democratic Party’s thinking on the topic. With many Democrats already jockeying for position ahead of the next presidential race, he outlined what he would do on A.I. if he were one of them.

“I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,’” he said, according to the transcript.

He contrasted the technology with other innovations that could be dangerous in the wrong hands, saying that unlike “nuclear power, you don’t need a bunch of highly enriched uranium” to build powerful A.I.

“I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what does it mean if there’s going to be job displacement,” Mr. Obama said, according to the transcript, adding, “if it turns out that you’ve got a lot more people who can’t find full-time work because they’ve been rendered redundant, how are we going to respond?”

item.title: How Candidates Have Addressed Affordability in the Midterm Campaigns
item.description:
Affordability has become the buzzword of the midterm campaigns.

Around the country, candidates are trying hard to relate to voters’ economic pain. But Republicans are handicapped by the grind of war, promises they made on inflation during the 2024 campaign and a president who alternatively insists that prices have declined and then dismisses the issue as a con job created by Democrats.

Democrats may still have to answer for inflation that hit a four-decade high as the Covid-19 pandemic was receding; Republicans continue to blame today’s economic woes on the Biden administration.

Though the overall economy is resilient — 162,000 jobs were added to the market in August — voters across the political divide rank the cost of living as a top issue in public polls. Even those who can comfortably cover the basics worry about their economic future.

“Candidates are responding to what people are feeling, what people know on a day-to-day basis and what they see at the grocery stores or gas station. You can’t out-message their reality,” said Todd Belt, a professor at George Washington University’s Graduate School of Political Management. “We are now seeing more specific, material ways the candidate plans to make things better.”

The basic pitch

Democrats seized on affordability as a five-alarm crisis, recasting an issue that helped propel Mr. Trump’s return to the White House into a midterm weakness for Republicans. Voters have expressed deep skepticism of President Trump’s handling of the economy.

In local, state and national races, candidates — both incumbents running on their records and newcomers with fresh approaches — are promising to lower the price of necessities such as groceries, gas, utilities, housing, child care and health care. Solutions include suspending gas taxes, imposing rent caps and renegotiating drug prices in government programs like Medicare.

They are going on “affordability tours,” speaking in small-town diners, craft breweries, steel mills and even picket lines to pitch their version of the American dream and hear firsthand the choices some voters are being forced to make to pay their bills.

Roy Cooper, a Democrat running for the Senate in North Carolina, calls his tour “Make Stuff Cost Less.” Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in Florida, refers to his as the “Defending the Florida Dream” tour. And in South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee for the Senate, is hosting a tour called “Gas, Grits and Groceries.”

With less than two months before the midterm elections, candidates are focusing on big-ticket necessities that have increased in price in recent years. The spikes, combined with stagnant wages have hit American workers hard. Here are examples of political ads and candidates speaking directly to voters:

Housing

Many midterm candidates have focused, at least in part, on how to bring down the price of housing — typically the biggest household budget item.

Since the start of the pandemic, the price of homes has climbed by around 50 percent. About a third of American households are “housing cost burdened,” meaning they spend more than 30 percent of their income on housing.

By last year, the median age of first-time home buyers had risen to 40 years old. And while rental prices have decreased in some markets, they are still more expensive than prepandemic levels. In June, Congress passed the first major legislative package to address the housing crisis in more than 30 years with strong bipartisan support, but its impact will take time.

Both Republicans and Democrats have promised a range of fixes including reforming bureaucratic permit processing to help build faster and reduce construction costs, and restricting the sale of single-family homes or rental housing to private equity firms.

Groceries

Groceries and gas, two of the most unavoidable reminders of cost-of-living increases, continue to take perhaps the most palpable toll on family budgets. Fuel prices that rose with the Iran war are again spiking, with the national average over $4 per gallon and diesel at a record high. Food prices are up by about 3 percent year over year, according to the Consumer Price Index.

The president’s tariffs have increased the cost of some imported food and farm implements. Counter tariffs imposed by trading partners have further strained farm budgets, raising the costs of meat and produce.

Candidates, particularly Democrats, are tapping into voter anger and linking some of the increases to what they characterize as corporate greed.

To drive down pricing, candidates are pushing to roll back the tariffs and local sales taxes on some food items, while questioning grocery store mergers and what they call price gouging. Others have focused on suspending gas taxes for relief, at least temporarily.

Child care

Working Americans have long struggled with the costs of child care. In recent years, the prices have skyrocketed as government funding drops, operating costs increase and child-care worker shortages arise, especially as the president cracks down on immigration.

Now, families earning the median income in every state spend far more than the 7 percent of household income that the Department of Health and Human Services considers affordable. In a 2025 poll by the American Family Survey, seven in 10 Americans said raising children is unaffordable, an increase of 13 percentage points over a year earlier.

Many candidates are framing the conversation as a work force issue that requires investment. Some Democrats are pushing for universal child care as a publicly funded solution. Some Republicans favor lowering costs through tax credits.

Health care

The price of getting sick has long loomed as a crushing threat for many Americans, but the issue was brought into sharp focus when Republicans lawmakers allowed enhanced government subsidies for health coverage under the Affordable Care Act to lapse. Many Americans’ insurance premiums more than doubled when the subsidies expired.

Health care costs are among the top economic concerns of voters across the political spectrum. Annual premiums for employer-covered family health coverage reached about $27,000 on average in 2025. Workers contributed $6,850 a year, on average toward the cost of family coverage, according to a survey by KFF, a health research group.

And changes to Medicaid eligibility, which were passed to help pay for spending and tax cuts in Mr. Trump’s signature domestic policy law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, could further strain family budgets.

Utilities

Over the past few years, millions of Americans have been hit with higher electricity bills — the result of complicated forces that are different from state to state. Residential electricity prices have risen 13 percent on average since 2022, according to the Energy Information Administration.

Republicans and Democrats point to different causes.

Republican candidates have proposed eliminating electrification mandates and prioritizing natural and domestically produced gas while opposing renewable energy as costly.

Democratic candidates have pinned the blame on energy-devouring data centers and pledged to stop them or build protections. They have also pushed to expand tax credits for wind, solar and other renewable energy sources to expand supply.

James Thomas contributed video production.

]]>

item.title: Is Florida Ready for Angie Nixon?
item.description:
Angie Nixon is tough to silence.

The first time she protested gerrymandering in Florida, Republican state lawmakers cut the video feed of her sit-in. The second time she showed up with a bullhorn. The third time, she was arrested.

“When they go low,” she says, putting a twist on Michelle Obama’s decade-old dictum, “we get loud.”

Ms. Nixon’s high-volume tactics as a state representative have made her one of the most outspoken critics of Florida’s Republican governor, Ron DeSantis. She has also at times rankled fellow Democrats. Some political veterans dismissed her campaign for the U.S. Senate as progressive whimsy — until her decisive primary victory against a more moderate opponent last month. It catapulted her onto the national stage and jolted an otherwise sleepy Democratic Party in a Republican-leaning state.

She has spent the weeks since hoarse, appearing nearly everywhere as she tries to make the case that a Black woman with a Southern drawl — who identifies as a progressive but also joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June — can win in a state President Trump has taken three times. If elected, Ms. Nixon would become Florida’s first Black senator.

National Democrats have all but written off Florida. Republicans believe the nomination of Ms. Nixon, whom they have branded a “socialist,” has only made it easier for Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent Mr. DeSantis appointed last year to replace Marco Rubio, to win in November.

But Ms. Nixon the Senate nominee, much like Ms. Nixon the state legislator, is difficult to ignore. She leans fiery while Ms. Moody leans restrained. She engages with the media and curious crowds drawn to her, while Ms. Moody mostly sticks to Fox News and friendly supporters.

The forces working against Republicans nationally — the high cost of living, some Hispanic voters who lean away from Mr. Trump — are also present in Florida. And Florida Democrats have historically turned out more voters with a Black candidate leading the ticket.

“What up, Nassau County!” Ms. Nixon, 42, told a full house of supporters recently in Yulee, a deep-red community in northeastern Florida, near Georgia. She later joked that they probably had never seen so many Democrats here.

The establishment Ms. Nixon is not. Her primary win so shocked some Democratic leaders that a unity rally, planned on the assumption that her rival would win, was scrapped. Some Jewish Democrats were upset by a resolution she filed in 2023 in Tallahassee calling for a cease-fire “in the State of Israel and occupied Palestine,” which failed with a vote of 104-2. She has since mended some fences and been quick to condemn antisemitic incidents.

She also does not quite fit the mold of other democratic socialists running this year. A longtime union and community organizer, she has been rooted in campaigns to restore felon voting rights, expand Medicaid and unionize adjunct college professors. She also owns a book-and-coffee shop named Cafe Resistance. In 2020, she received the endorsement of the chamber of commerce in Jacksonville, her hometown, and then ousted a conservative Democratic incumbent.

Her vocal opposition to Mr. DeSantis has become her calling card. At every turn of his administration’s “war on woke” — changing how slavery was taught in schools, restricting diversity initiatives, removing books from school libraries — Ms. Nixon was there, calling the policies racist and the governor a bully. Her shop showcases banned books.

When Mr. DeSantis was booed at a vigil in 2023 for Black victims killed in a racially motivated shooting in a Jacksonville Dollar General store, she stood nearby, arms at her hips, glowering at him.

This spring, she parked herself in the governor’s office and demanded a meeting over his administration’s gerrymandered congressional map. She refused to leave, leading to her arrest. She is awaiting trial next month on trespassing charges.

“I’m the biggest pain in Ron DeSantis’s ass,” she recently told donors at a fund-raiser in Miami, casting herself as the fighter voters want and saying she would be the “biggest pain” for Mr. Trump, too. For his part, the president called her a “card-carrying member” of the D.S.A. at his Republican midterm convention last week.

Some Democrats dislike her style and politics, but Ms. Nixon comes off as authentic, something Florida Democrats have struggled with, said Joe Garcia, a former Miami congressman, who co-hosted the fund-raiser.

“You may not like what she’s saying, but you know it’s what she feels,” he said. “It’s very powerful.”

Daniel Henry, the first vice chairman of the Florida Democratic Party, who has worked closely with Ms. Nixon, said her skeptics dismissed her passion and organizing skills at their peril.

“The people that usually underestimate her,” he said, “end up losing.”

Ms. Nixon was raised in Jacksonville’s historically Black Montcrief neighborhood. Her mother worked two jobs to support her and her brother.

At 13, Ms. Nixon said in her hometown newspaper, The Florida Times-Union, that she would call a movie based on her life “Outspoken,” “because I like to tell how I feel inside and not just leave things bottled up.”

She graduated from Stanton College Preparatory, a public magnet high school, and from the University of Florida. In her final semester, a visibly pregnant Ms. Nixon walked into the office of Mia L. Jones, then a Jacksonville city councilwoman, and asked to be her intern. The City Council did not offer internships.

“She was not afraid to come and ask for something that didn’t exist,” said Ms. Jones, who created one for her.

In 2008, barely out of college and a single mother to her 1-year-old daughter, Ms. Nixon ran for the City Council. The Times-Union endorsed her — “Her moxie certainly isn’t in doubt,” the editorial board wrote — but she lost the election.

A few years later, when her daughter, Natalie McGriff, felt insecure about her looks, the mother and daughter published children’s books about “Moxie McGriff,” whose curly hair gave her superpowers.

Ms. Nixon sometimes struggled financially. Public records show that her home was briefly in foreclosure in 2014, when she was between jobs and behind on mortgage payments. The case was later dismissed.

In 2016, she worked as the deputy field director for national Black outreach for Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaign. Four years later, Ms. Nixon has said, she supported Elizabeth Warren for the Democratic nomination.

That year, Ms. Nixon ran for the State House while pregnant with her younger daughter. Democrats had all but shut down field campaigns because of the coronavirus pandemic, recalled Andrea Cristina Mercado, a fellow progressive organizer. Ms. Nixon insisted on canvassing anyway, contracting Covid before the election.

“Angie kept being a voice of like, ‘Republicans are out there on those doors,’” Ms. Mercado said. “‘We have to be out there on those doors, too.’”

After winning in a rout, Ms. Nixon married Jarrett Morene, the father of her younger daughter. Their blended families made them parents of five children.

Ms. Nixon arrived at the State Capitol as Mr. DeSantis was becoming a national Republican darling. In 2022, Republican lawmakers prepared to pass redistricting maps that diluted Black representation. Ms. Nixon and State Representative Travaris McCurdy interrupted the session and sat on the House floor in protest. They wore “STOP THE BLACK ATTACK” T-shirts, which they had raced to the local mall to make the night before.

The sit-in turned Ms. Nixon into a foil for the powerful Mr. DeSantis. But it also brought criticism.

In 2024, her primary opponent accused her of failing to pass legislation or secure money for district projects. Ms. Nixon, who worked in the Legislature to expand child care and confront price gouging, countered that Republicans wanted her gone because she was “making too much noise.”

She won with 81 percent of the vote.

This year, when Republican lawmakers readied a vote on a new set of congressional maps that eliminated four Democratic seats, Ms. Nixon was running for Senate.

She procured a pink bullhorn — the color of her campaign signs — and wore a matching jumpsuit as she marched down the center aisle of the House floor in protest. A couple of weeks later, she staged her sit-in inside Mr. DeSantis’s office.

Republicans and some Democrats dismissed her protests as stunts. Democratic primary voters felt differently, choosing her by double digits over Alex Vindman, a former national security official with party establishment ties.

Winning a general election is harder. Ms. Moody is something of a generic Republican, but that has been enough for Florida, where Republicans now handily outnumber Democrats. Florida is not on any list of competitive Senate races, though a strong showing from Ms. Nixon could lift other Democrats down the ballot.

Ms. Moody has declined to debate Ms. Nixon, saying she is “not going to give a stage or any attention” to someone she considers “truly anti-American.” She has alluded to past speeches that Ms. Nixon gave to the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a Muslim advocacy and civil rights group that Florida has declared a foreign terrorist organization.

Mr. DeSantis has flatly dismissed a democratic socialist’s chances in Florida: “I don’t think it’s going to work at all.”

The idea that a grass-roots focus on working people could energize voters originated with Ms. Nixon and her brain trust of labor organizers, including Alphonso Mayfield, the late leader of the Florida Public Services Union, and her former boss. Mr. Mayfield, who died in January, was perhaps Ms. Nixon’s biggest champion.

Ms. Nixon campaigns in a van, nicknamed the Vangie, that is filled with snacks, a clothes rack and a pillow. To save money, she often stays with friends and family. Her most recent financial disclosure listed a nearly $14,000 debt to the I.R.S., which her campaign said was a tax payment plan.

Her events are intended to recruit supporters as canvassers and phone bankers. Her speeches sound like church revivals, with Ms. Nixon leading call-and-response chants, as she did on a recent rainy Saturday in Miami’s Little Havana neighborhood.

“I am running against a woman that voted to end health care for 440,000 Floridians in this state — say, ‘Shame!’” she said.

A democratic socialist is a tough sell in South Florida, particularly among Hispanics. Ms. Nixon does not regret her D.S.A. membership, saying she is a big-tent Democrat, but while in Miami she denounced authoritarian leaders in Cuba and Venezuela. She then hopped in her van and knocked on doors.

Jesús García, a 60-year-old bus driver who emigrated from Cuba, welcomed Ms. Nixon into his living room, telling her he recognized her from TikTok.

“What you’re doing is great,” said Mr. García, a naturalized citizen registered without party affiliation, who described himself as liberal. “Are you a progressive? A socialist?”

“I’m a progressive,” Ms. Nixon said. “I don’t go by labels.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

]]>

item.title: Top Lawmakers Agree A.I.’s Risks Are Rising but Say They Have No Quick Fix
item.description:
As warnings rapidly mount over the pace and potential dangers of artificial intelligence development, the top Republican and Democrat in the House agreed on Sunday that Congress should put guardrails in place, but would not commit to specific policies or a timeline for doing so.

Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, urged caution in an interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” saying that the House could not hastily pass regulations and that lawmakers needed to ensure American companies remain competitive with Chinese A.I. firms.

“We’re not going to rush in and pass a piece of legislation that would do harm to the country and put China at an edge,” Mr. Johnson, who controls what legislation comes to the House floor, said. “And so we’ve got to do this carefully.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, criticized Mr. Johnson for moving too slowly, saying in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” that the House should take “decisive action.” But when he was asked for specific restrictions that he might back, Mr. Jeffries would not elaborate.

“Well, we’ll have that conversation this week upon our return,” he said. Mr. Jeffries is considered the leading contender to become speaker if Democrats take control of the House after the midterm elections.

The House will return to Washington on Monday for what is scheduled to be its final week in session before November’s midterm elections, a short timeline that makes it nearly impossible for lawmakers to quickly adopt a comprehensive framework for A.I. regulations.

Though politicians from both parties have warned about the need to regulate A.I. development, the drumbeat of ominous warnings about the technology has increased significantly in recent weeks. Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, resigned on Tuesday, saying in social media posts that he believed that the top A.I. companies were not developing the technology responsibly.

On Saturday, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, called for tech companies to slow the pace of their development in the face of worries about the technology’s safety. Several other tech executives — including Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, the billionaire whose company SpaceX has been increasing its spending on A.I. — said they backed that effort.

Worries over A.I.’s dangers are rising as an issue in the midterm elections, and former President Barack Obama, in a fund-raising event last week, implored Democrats to develop clear positions on how to address risks the technology poses to safety and the economy.

Mr. Johnson acknowledged the issue was significant. But he pointed out that even Mr. Amodei and his competitors did not agree on the best approach and said that they should play a part in the development of any regulatory framework.

“I think the first step is to have a meeting of all the platform providers,” he said. “I’ve talked to the president about this and others. I believe that’s the next step.”

Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, said on “Fox News Sunday” that the Trump administration was “studying” efforts on Capitol Hill to regulate A.I., including a push to create a “kill switch” that would allow the government to order rogue models to be shut down.

But even as he acknowledged that A.I. has advanced so rapidly that it is capable of undermining existing cybersecurity protections, Mr. Hassett joined Mr. Johnson in endorsing the involvement of the private sector in any efforts to slow the pace of development.

Mr. Johnson also warned that any excessive regulations on A.I. risked restraining American companies and empowering Chinese firms, an argument that President Trump also made on Sunday when speaking to reporters in Ireland, where he was attending a tournament at one of his golf resorts.

“Look, we’re leading China in A.I.,” Mr. Trump said. “We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up. And they’re bringing up things that won’t happen. But whoever wins with A.I., wins.”

Many Democrats have argued that Congress should not be letting tech executives take the lead in regulating their own technology. After Mr. Johnson declined to renew a bipartisan task force on artificial intelligence, House Democrats established their own A.I. commission that Mr. Jeffries said would soon present “an aggressive framework.”

A group of lawmakers also circulated a letter last week urging Mr. Johnson to cancel their scheduled recess until lawmakers advanced A.I. regulations.

Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said in a CNN interview that Congress was moving too slowly to address the issue. He also dismissed concerns over China.

“We can’t just use this idea that if we do this we somehow are going to lose to China,” Mr. Gallego said on “State of the Union.” “Because A.I. does not care once it becomes fully dangerous whether we’re Chinese or American. That’s the danger of this.”

Ian Fisher contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Texas Republican’s Racist Social Media Post Draws Condemnation
item.description:
The video captured a moment of jubilation familiar to any college sports fan.

A sea of burnt-orange-clad students erupted in whoops and hollers after the Texas Longhorns’ game-winning touchdown on Saturday night, jumping up and down, hugging one another, tossing drinks in the air.

By Sunday, the scene had become a powder keg for Texas Republicans, after the G.O.P. nominee for a statewide office captioned a screenshot of the celebration with a racist message on social media.

“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” the nominee, Bo French, who is running for a spot on a powerful state agency that regulates oil and gas, wrote in a post on X that showed cheering fans of color. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” He later posted a complaint about the admission of foreign students at the University of Texas, seeming to assume they could not have been born in the state because of their skin color.

Numerous Texas Republicans condemned the post. Some distanced themselves without explicitly denouncing it. And a handful of others responded to a Republican senator’s disapproval of the post by castigating the senator.

Democrats roundly criticized the post, and some argued that the Republican responses did not go far enough. The uproar came as both parties are in heated midterm competitions across the state, which has navigated flare-ups of Islamophobia and tense debates over immigration.

Mr. French, who is running for the state Railroad Commission, has a history of making anti-Muslim, antisemitic and anti-immigrant comments. He faced criticism last year after sharing a poll on social media asking who was the “bigger threat” to America, Muslims or Jews. The reactions from many Republicans to Mr. French’s post on Sunday reflected the discomfort they have with his candidacy.

“Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized,” Senator John Cornyn, a Republican, wrote on X in response to Mr. French’s post about the football game. “This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad.”

State Representative Dustin Burrows, a Republican who is the House speaker, wrote: “Delete it.” Mr. Burrows said, “You can oppose immigration policy without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity — this post has crossed the line.”

State Representative Lacey Hull, a Republican who leads the House committee on Human Services, wrote, “This post breaks my heart.” She added, “I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans.”

After a campaign that demonized Muslims and immigrants, Mr. French narrowly won his primary against Jim Wright, the Railroad Commission’s chairman, in May — despite opposition from prominent Republicans like Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and others.

Mr. Abbott, who is running for re-election, said in a statement that Mr. French’s post was “not my message.” He added, “A selective picture of Longhorn fans celebrating our biggest home victory — ever — actually shows a way that Texans unite.” Mr. Abbott then praised strict immigration laws and nodded to his move to block Texas public universities from using skilled foreign worker visas, known as H-1Bs.

In a reply to his original post on Sunday, Mr. French wrote, “I weep for the families in Texas who can’t get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans.” Yet state law requires that Texas high school students who were ranked in the top 10 percent of their class be automatically admitted, and that they compose up to 75 percent of the class. International students make up fewer than 10 percent of the student body, according to statistics that the University of Texas released in September.

Democrats rushed to condemn Mr. French’s comments, including State Representative James Talarico, a nominee for Senate. He called on his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, Texas’ attorney general, to do the same.

Mr. Paxton turned the request back on his opponent and did not directly address Mr. French’s post.

“I condemn racism in all its forms,” Mr. Paxton wrote on X, adding, “Only one person in this race has a history of dividing Texans by race, and it’s James Talarico.”

State Representative Andy Hopper, a hard-line conservative, responded to Mr. Cornyn’s post about Mr. French by calling Mr. Cornyn a “smug globalist” and highlighting his landslide loss to Mr. Paxton in the Senate primary.

Mr. French has a strong chance to win in November, given the state’s Republican lean. But his candidacy has given his Democratic opponent, State Representative Jon Rosenthal, newfound hope.

In a phone interview, Mr. Rosenthal criticized Mr. Abbott, who he said was “feeding the problem instead of pushing back on it” by invoking foreign worker visas in response to Mr. French’s post.

He rejected Mr. French’s comments.

“Most of the voters that I talk to are tired of the hatefulness and division,” Mr. Rosenthal said, adding, “There’s a small segment of society that revels in hate, and I hope they end up being relegated to irrelevance."

If Mr. French is elected, he may continue to face resistance from his fellow Republicans. The chair of a committee that oversees the state oil and gas commission, State Representative Drew Darby, said the Legislature could circumscribe Mr. French’s power if he stepped out of line.
